Indian Geography - Class Notes | 15 November 2026

Topics: the seasons of India; the winter (cold weather) season: how it forms (sun, continentality, pressure, ITCZ shift, NE trades, the westerly jet and the Himalayan barrier), temperature, pressure, winds, the subtropical westerly jet, cold waves and western disturbances (mechanism, significance and the effect of climate change); and the summer (hot weather) season: the loo, dust and thunderstorms, heat waves, heat domes and omega blocks, and heat-wave policy.

Class date: 15 November 2026. This class follows the monsoon mechanism notes of 13 November (jet streams, Tibet, ENSO) and 14 November (La Nina, IOD, MJO, human influences). Sections, maps, figures and correction ids restart at 1.

Labels: [Correction] marks a substantive change to the rough notes; [Additional] marks relevant supporting material; [Verification Required] flags claims that could not be confirmed; [Current Affairs] marks dated news (as of 16 November 2026); † marks a standard fact not re-checked against a page opened for this note. Maps are schematic (simplified Natural Earth data) and diagrams are conceptual. Time-sensitive figures carry their year and source.

1. Seasons of India

India has a tropical monsoon climate, so its year is divided by the seasonal reversal of winds and rain, not by the four temperate seasons. Two schemes are in use, and both appear in exams.

SeasonIMD meteorological seasonsTraditional scheme (NCERT, older books)Main feature
Winter (cold weather)January-FebruaryDecember-February (in the north from mid-November)Cold, dry north-easterly/north-westerly land winds; western disturbances
Summer (hot weather, pre-monsoon)March-MayMarch-May (June in the north-west)Rising heat, thermal low, loo, local storms
Rainy (south-west monsoon)June-SeptemberJune-SeptemberAbout three-quarters of annual rain†
Post-monsoon (retreating monsoon)October-DecemberOctober-NovemberWithdrawal of SW monsoon; NE monsoon rain in Tamil Nadu; cyclones
[Correction] The notes give "according to IMD: winter Dec-Feb ... retreating monsoon Oct-Nov". IMD's meteorological seasons are Winter: January-February; Pre-monsoon: March-May; Southwest monsoon: June-September; Post-monsoon: October-December (IMD glossary). The Dec-Feb / Oct-Nov version is the traditional (NCERT) scheme. In answers, name the scheme you are using; for an IMD question, use Jan-Feb and Oct-Dec.

2. The Winter (Cold Weather) Season

2.1 Temperature

  • Around 22 December the sun is overhead the Tropic of Capricorn, so India receives its weakest sunshine of the year. December-January are the coldest months in the northern plains.
  • North India is cold because of continentality: Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan lie far from the sea, so they lose heat quickly on long, clear winter nights. Snowfall on the nearby Himalaya and cold north-westerly winds add to this. Night temperatures can fall below freezing in Punjab and Rajasthan.
  • South India stays mild because of the moderating (maritime) influence of the sea and its nearness to the equator. The Peninsula has no well-defined cold season.
  • Temperature decreases from south to north. NCERT gives mean January temperatures of about 24-25°C at Chennai and 10-15°C in the northern plains†.
  • Isotherm: the January 20°C isotherm runs roughly parallel to the Tropic of Cancer, through the middle of the country, as the notes say ("20° line in the centre of India")†.
    [Additional] Do not confuse it with the 18°C January isotherm, which L.D. Stamp used to divide India into a tropical south and a sub-tropical (temperate) north. This was asked in UPSC Prelims (see PYQ 4).
  • Why India is warmer than other places at the same latitude: the Himalaya blocks the bitterly cold Siberian/Central Asian air. This is why even sub-tropical north India keeps a largely tropical character (see the 12 November note).

2.2 Pressure, Winds and Stable Air

  • Surface high pressure: cold, dense air over north-west India and Central Asia creates high pressure. Under the jet stream, air also sinks (subsides) from the upper troposphere. Sinking air warms by compression and dries out, so it inhibits cloud and rain.
  • Anticyclonic, stable conditions: the pressure gradient is weak, so winds are light (about 3-5 km/h†). Calm, clear nights create a temperature inversion (cold air at the surface, warmer air above). This traps fog and pollution, which is why the Indo-Gangetic plain suffers smog in winter.
  • Surface winds blow outward from the land: westerly/north-westerly down the Ganga valley, northerly over the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, and north-easterly over the Bay of Bengal. They are cold and dry, so most of India gets no rain.
  • Exception: Tamil Nadu (Coromandel) coast. The north-easterlies pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and give the north-east monsoon rain (October-December), the main rainy season of coastal Tamil Nadu.
  • Upper air: the subtropical westerly jet (STWJ). In winter the jet moves south and is split by the Tibetan Plateau. Its southern branch flows west to east south of the Himalaya at about 9-13 km (mean position about 25°N†). It (a) helps keep the surface high by making air sink and (b) steers western disturbances into India. Formation and the split are in the 13 November note, 2.3.

2.3 Cold Waves

  • A cold wave is an abnormally cold spell, dangerous to life (hypothermia, frostbite), crops (frost) and livestock.
  • Causes: very cold, dry north-westerly winds after a western disturbance passes; clear skies that allow strong night cooling; fresh snow on the nearby hills; and occasionally cold air from Central Asia that crosses the Hindu Kush and western passes.
    [Correction] The notes say cold waves come from "north-westerly winds bringing extra cold air of Central Asia - Hindu Kush". This is only part of it. The Himalaya blocks most Siberian air. Most north Indian cold waves follow the passage of a western disturbance: winds turn cold and north-westerly, skies clear, and the fresh snow on the hills chills the air. Clear, calm nights then cool the ground sharply (radiational cooling).
IMD criterion (plains)Cold waveSevere cold wave
Pre-conditionMinimum temperature 10°C or less (plains); 0°C or less (hills)
By departure from normal (minimum temperature)-4.5°C to -6.4°Cmore than -6.4°C
By actual minimum temperature (plains only)4°C or less2°C or less
Coastal stationsDeparture -4.5°C or more, with minimum 15°C or less
Cold day (a separate term)Minimum 10°C or less and maximum 4.5-6.4°C below normal (severe: more than 6.4°C below). Usually caused by fog or low cloud that blocks sunlight all day.

Source: IMD - FAQ on Cold Wave. A cold wave is declared when the criteria are met at 2 or more stations in a sub-division for 2 consecutive days.

[Additional] Frost and cold wave are on the list of notified calamities for State and National Disaster Response Fund (SDRF/NDRF) relief. NCDC lists 17 states/UTs in the core cold-wave zone, from Jammu and Kashmir to Telangana; J&K has the most cold waves, followed by Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Bihar, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh (NCDC advisory).

2.4 How the Winter Season Forms: The Complete Theory [Additional]

Sections 2.1-2.3 describe what winter looks like. This section explains why it forms, step by step, from the sun's position down to the weather in a north Indian village. Learn it as a chain: each link causes the next.

1. Sun moves south → 2. Land cools fast (continentality) → 3. High pressure over Asia and NW India → 4. ITCZ shifts south of the equator → 5. NE trades return (winter monsoon) → 6. STWJ moves south, splits at Tibet, air sinks → 7. Dry, clear, stable weather, broken by WDs; rain only on the Coromandel coast

Step 1 - The astronomical control: the sun moves south

  • After the autumn equinox (about 23 September) the overhead sun moves into the southern hemisphere and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn on about 22 December (winter solstice).
  • Two things reduce the heat India receives:
    1. Lower sun angle. The noon sun at Delhi (28.6°N) stands only about 38° above the horizon on 22 December, against about 85° on 21 June. The same beam spreads over a larger area and passes through more atmosphere. Per unit of ground, Delhi gets only about 60% of its June noon intensity. (Calculated: altitude = 90° - (latitude + 23.4°); intensity is proportional to the sine of the altitude.) Chennai (13°N) still has a noon sun of about 53°, which is one reason the south stays warm.
    2. Shorter days, longer nights. Delhi has roughly 10 hours 20 minutes of daylight in late December, against about 14 hours in June†. Long nights give the ground more time to lose heat.
  • The effect grows with latitude, so it is strongest in the north. This alone explains why temperature decreases from south to north (2.1).

Step 2 - The thermal control: land cools faster than sea

  • Specific heat: water needs about four to five times as much energy as dry soil to change temperature by the same amount†. Water also mixes heat down to tens of metres, and land only through a thin top layer. So when sunshine weakens, the Asian landmass cools much faster than the Indian Ocean. In summer this contrast drives moist air onto land; in winter it reverses. This is the basic "seasonal reversal" behind the word monsoon (see the thermal concept in the 12 November note).
  • Continentality: places far from the sea (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, west UP) have no moderating sea breeze and dry air, so they have the coldest nights and the largest daily range. Coastal Kerala and the Andamans barely change.
  • Radiational (nocturnal) cooling: on clear, calm, dry nights the ground radiates long-wave heat straight to space. Dry air holds little water vapour, so there is little greenhouse "blanket" to send heat back. Cloud-free nights are therefore the coldest. One cloudy night (for example, ahead of a WD) can raise the minimum temperature by several degrees.
  • Snow cover on the Himalaya after each WD reflects sunlight (high albedo) and chills the air that drains down to the plains.

Step 3 - The pressure field: cold air makes high pressure

  • Cold air is dense and contracts, so it builds high surface pressure. Over Siberia and Mongolia this forms the Siberian-Mongolian High, the strongest surface high pressure on Earth in winter (central pressure often above 1,030-1,040 hPa†). It is shallow: the cold air is only a few kilometres deep.
  • A much weaker secondary high forms over north-west India (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, the upper Indus and Ganga valleys). NCERT gives the 1019 mb isobar over north-west India and the 1013 mb isobar in the far south†.
  • Pressure is lower over the warmer Indian Ocean, and lowest in the equatorial trough south of the equator and over northern Australia. Air therefore tends to flow from north to south: from land to sea.
  • The gradient over India is small (about 6 mb across the whole country), so winds are only about 3-5 km/h. Calm air is one reason fog and smog sit still for days.
  • Role of the Himalaya: because the Siberian cold air is shallow, the Himalaya (average height over 6,000 m) and the Tibetan Plateau block it. India's winter is therefore far milder than places at the same latitude in East Asia, which receive Siberian outbreaks directly. Some cold air still leaks in from the north-west, through the lower ranges and passes of Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Step 4 - The planetary control: the ITCZ shifts south

  • The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is the belt where the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet and air rises. It follows the overhead sun, with a lag. In July it lies over north India as the monsoon trough (about 20-25°N). In January it has moved to about 5-15°S over the Indian Ocean and northern Australia† (Map 2, Figure 2).
  • The whole system of pressure belts moves south with it (NCERT: "in the northern hemisphere in winter they move southwards"). North India comes under the descending limb of the Hadley cell: the air that rises at the ITCZ flows north aloft and sinks over north India and the subtropics.
  • Sinking air is compressed and warms (about 10°C per km, the dry adiabatic rate), so its relative humidity falls. No cloud can form in sinking air. This is the main dynamic reason why winter is dry.

Step 5 - The surface winds: the NE trades return (the winter or north-east monsoon)

  • With the ITCZ south of the equator, India comes under the north-east trade winds. Air flows out of the north-west Indian high towards the low pressure in the south, and the Coriolis force (deflection to the right in the northern hemisphere) turns it into a north-easterly wind. This is the winter monsoon or north-east monsoon.
  • Relief changes the direction locally: westerly or north-westerly down the Ganga valley (channelled between the Himalaya and the Peninsula), northerly over the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, and truly north-easterly only over the open Bay of Bengal.
  • Two air streams meet in the north-west. NCERT notes that dry continental air from the Central Asian high meets the trade winds over north-west India. The meeting zone is not fixed; it sometimes moves east to the middle Ganga valley, putting all of north and north-west India under dry north-westerly winds†.
  • After crossing the equator the same air is deflected to the left (southern hemisphere) and becomes the north-west monsoon of Indonesia and northern Australia. Their rainy season is our dry season, the mirror image of the south-west monsoon (Map 2).
  • Why these winds give no rain over most of India: (a) they start over land, so they are dry; (b) they are cold and sinking, so the air is stable; (c) they blow offshore, from land to sea; (d) they diverge out of a high-pressure area instead of converging into a low. Rain needs moisture plus rising air, and the winter monsoon has neither.
  • The one exception - the Coromandel coast: the north-easterlies cross several hundred kilometres of the warm Bay of Bengal and pick up moisture. They meet the Tamil Nadu coast almost head-on and are lifted by convergence at the coast and by the Eastern Ghats hills. Low-pressure systems and cyclones in the Bay add to this. Result: Tamil Nadu receives about 48% of its annual rain in October-December†, and coastal districts more. Tamil Nadu is relatively dry in June-September because it lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.

Step 6 - The upper-air control: the subtropical westerly jet

  • In winter the pole-to-equator temperature contrast is strongest. By the thermal wind principle, a stronger temperature contrast gives stronger westerly winds aloft, so the subtropical westerly jet (STWJ) is at its strongest and lies furthest south.
  • It appears over north India in October, after the south-west monsoon withdraws, and moves further south as winter advances. The Tibetan Plateau splits it into a northern branch (north of Tibet) and a southern branch (south of the Himalaya, mean position about 25°N, 9-13 km high). The branches rejoin over China and Japan.
  • The southern branch does three jobs:
    1. Subsidence: air converging at the jet's entrance sinks below it. This strengthens the surface high and the temperature inversion, and keeps the sky clear (Figure 1).
    2. Steering western disturbances into India from the Mediterranean (section 3).
    3. Timing the seasons: its northward retreat in late May-June removes the "lid" over north India and allows the south-west monsoon to arrive (13 November note, Koteshwaram's view).

Step 7 - Interruptions: western disturbances, cold waves and Bay systems

  • The calm, clear pattern is broken every few days by western disturbances (roughly 6-7 a month in winter†). Each one gives a sequence: clouds and milder nights → rain on the plains, snow on the hills → cold, dry north-westerlies, clear skies, a cold wave and dense fog (section 3, Figure 3).
  • Intense cold waves are linked to an omega block over the Ural-Siberian region, which lets cold northerlies flow into north India (Athira et al., 2024, Weather and Climate Extremes).
  • In the south, low-pressure areas, depressions and cyclones of the Bay of Bengal (October-December) give most of the north-east monsoon rain to Tamil Nadu, south Andhra Pradesh and Sri Lanka.

Exam point - old versus modern explanation. The old textbook view treats the winter monsoon as a giant land breeze blowing from cold Asia to the warm ocean (Halley's thermal concept). The modern view keeps the land-sea contrast but adds: (1) the southward shift of the ITCZ and the pressure belts, which brings back the NE trades; (2) the Hadley-cell subsidence over north India; and (3) the southern branch of the STWJ, which causes sinking air and steers WDs. Write all three in a Mains answer.

2.6 Year-to-Year Variation: ENSO, IOD and a Warming Climate

  • El Nino and La Nina affect Indian winters too. An IMD study of cold waves (December-February, 86 stations, 1971-2020) found that El Nino mostly inhibits cold-wave activity and La Nina has the opposite effect (Pai and Nair, MAUSAM 2022). Athira et al. (2024) also found more frequent and longer cold waves in La Nina winters.
  • Long-term trend: the same studies report decreasing cold-wave days at many stations, because winter minimum temperatures are rising with global warming. Winter rain has become more erratic (see 3.4).
  • North-east monsoon and ENSO: El Nino years have often (but not always) brought good north-east monsoon rain to Tamil Nadu†, the reverse of its effect on the south-west monsoon. This link is weak, so do not treat it as a rule.
[Current Affairs] Winter 2026-27 begins under a very strong El Nino (as of 16 November 2026).
  • IMD's outlook for November 2026 (issued 31 October 2026) says very strong El Nino conditions prevail and are likely to continue through November-December, with a neutral IOD. It expects above-normal minimum temperatures over most of India, except many parts of central and eastern India (IMD press release).
  • November rain over South Peninsular India is forecast to be below normal (under 77% of the LPA of about 118.7 mm), which means a weak start to the north-east monsoon despite El Nino.
  • IMD's extended-range forecast of 12 November 2026 reported rainfall 32% below normal for the country from 1 October to 11 November, heavy rain in coastal Andhra Pradesh and Telangana from the remnant of Severe Cyclonic Storm "Murasu", and a western disturbance over Kashmir bringing rain and hail on 12-13 November.
  • Exam use: an El Nino winter favours a milder winter with fewer cold waves, but this is a tendency, not a certainty. IMD will issue its December-February outlook at the end of November 2026.

2.7 Model Answer: Explain the Mechanism of the Winter Season in India

Introduction. The cold-weather season (traditionally mid-November to February; IMD: January-February) is the dry phase of India's monsoon climate, when the winds reverse and blow from land to sea.

Mechanism.

  1. Insolation: the overhead sun is over the Tropic of Capricorn (22 December), so the sun angle is low and days are short, especially in the north.
  2. Continentality: the Asian landmass cools faster than the Indian Ocean; clear, dry nights cause strong radiational cooling.
  3. Pressure: the Siberian High forms over Central Asia and a weak high over north-west India (about 1019 mb), with lower pressure over the ocean (about 1013 mb in the south).
  4. Planetary shift: the ITCZ moves south of the equator; north India lies under the sinking limb of the Hadley cell.
  5. Winds: the NE trades (winter monsoon) blow offshore. They are dry, light and stable, and are guided by relief (NW in the Ganga valley, NE over the Bay).
  6. Upper air: the southern branch of the STWJ (about 25°N) causes subsidence, an inversion and fog, and steers western disturbances.
  7. Barrier: the Himalaya blocks Siberian cold air, keeping India warmer than other places at the same latitude.

Outcome. Clear, dry, pleasant weather, with temperature falling from south to north. It is interrupted by WDs (rain and snow, then cold waves and fog) in the north-west. The north-east monsoon brings rain to the Coromandel coast.

Significance. Winter rain for rabi crops; snowpack for Himalayan rivers; hazards from cold waves, fog (transport) and smog (health).

Conclusion. Winter is a product of the same planetary system as the monsoon, shifted south. Climate change and ENSO are now altering its cold waves and rainfall, which calls for better forecasting and cold-wave action plans.

3. Western Disturbances (WDs)

3.1 What They Are

  • Definition: western disturbances are extra-tropical (mid-latitude, temperate) cyclonic systems that form over the Mediterranean region and travel east along the subtropical westerly jet to Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan and north-west India. Scientifically they are upper-air troughs in the westerly jet, often with a low or cyclonic circulation lower down (Hunt, 2024).
  • Moisture: from the Mediterranean, and on the way from the Black Sea and Caspian Sea; nearer India many also draw moisture from the Arabian Sea.
  • Frequency: on average six to seven strong WDs cross the subcontinent each winter month (Hunt, 2024, citing earlier studies). They are most common from December to March.
  • Weather: rain on the plains (Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, west Uttar Pradesh, north Rajasthan) and snow on Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Strong WDs reach Bihar, the north-east and Nepal.
[Correction] The notes call a WD a "low pressure condition, moist air, also called depression". Older books did call them "western depressions", but in IMD usage a depression is a specific stage of a tropical low (winds of 17-27 knots†). A WD is an extra-tropical (temperate) cyclonic system: an upper-air trough in the westerlies. It is not a tropical depression.

3.2 Mechanism of Western Disturbances

The class asked for this discussion.

  1. The jet as a wave. The subtropical westerly jet does not flow straight. It meanders north and south in long waves (Rossby waves). The northward bulge is a ridge (high pressure aloft) and the southward dip is a trough (low pressure aloft).
    [Correction] The notes write "Crest - Trough -> Ridge". In a jet wave the crest and the ridge are the same thing (the poleward bulge, high pressure aloft). The opposite is the trough (equatorward dip, low pressure aloft). A WD is linked to the trough.
  2. Birth over the Mediterranean. Cold air from Europe meets warmer, moist Mediterranean air. Instability in the jet deepens a trough there, and a low forms. Because it forms from the meeting of cold and warm air masses (fronts), it is a temperate (extra-tropical) cyclone.
  3. Carried east by the jet. The STWJ acts as a conveyor belt. In winter its southern branch lies south of the Himalaya, so it carries these troughs across Iraq, Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan to India in a few days.
  4. Picking up moisture. Over the Mediterranean, Black and Caspian Seas and, close to India, the Arabian Sea, the system gathers moisture.
  5. Uplift over India. Ahead of the trough, warm moist air is drawn in and rises (cyclonic convergence plus divergence aloft). The Himalaya forces it up further (orographic lift): snow falls on the mountains and rain on the plains.
  6. After passage. Behind the trough, cold dry north-westerly air flows in. Skies clear, so a cold wave, frost and dense fog follow. Then the next WD arrives, so the winter has a rhythm of cloudy-wet and clear-cold spells.
Mediterranean trough/low → carried east by STWJ → moisture from Med, Black, Caspian, Arabian Seas → lift over NW India + Himalaya → rain (plains) / snow (hills) → cold NW winds, cold wave, fog

3.3 Significance of Western Disturbances in Winter

AreaBenefit
AgricultureWinter rain (locally called mahawat†) is vital for rabi crops: wheat, barley, mustard, gram. It saves irrigation and helps grain filling.
Air qualityRain and wind wash out smog from the Indo-Gangetic plain (Delhi-NCR).
Water securitySnow on the western Himalaya melts slowly in spring and summer, feeding the Indus, Ganga and their tributaries, recharging springs and keeping glaciers healthy. IMD data: north-west India gets about 18% of its annual rain in January-March, and J&K-Ladakh about 31% (reported by TOI, January 2026).
HydropowerSnowmelt keeps up lean-season flows for Himalayan hydro projects.
TourismSnow brings winter tourists to Gulmarg, Auli, Manali and Shimla.
Following summerA wet winter with good snow cover and moist soils can delay or soften early-summer heat.
[Verification Required] The notes say this means "fewer heat waves". It is a reasonable tendency, but no IMD statement was found that a wet winter reduces heat waves.
Hazards too: WDs also bring hailstorms that flatten standing wheat, avalanches, landslides and road closures in the hills, cold waves and fog (transport delays), and, when they meet the monsoon in June-July, extreme rain and floods (Kedarnath 2013; north India July 2023; Himachal-Punjab 2025).

3.4 Climate Change and Western Disturbances

  • What the notes say: the frequency of WDs is falling; winter rain and snowfall are falling. The Arctic is warming fastest, which weakens the jet; a slower jet meanders more, giving weaker WDs. WDs are also arriving late (May-June) and interacting with the monsoon.
  • What the evidence shows:
    • Frequency has not clearly fallen. A review of 17 studies found no consensus on trends. The most detailed study (Hunt, 2024; 70 years of ERA5 data) found that winter WDs over the western and central Himalaya and the Hindu Kush have increased significantly, because the subtropical jet has strengthened.
    • The WD season has lengthened. WDs are now far more common in May, June and July. WDs were twice as common in June in the last 20 years as in the previous 50, because the jet now retreats north later. So WD-monsoon interactions (Kedarnath 2013, north India 2023) are becoming more frequent. This supports the notes' last point.
    • Winter precipitation has often failed recently. Several recent winters were very dry (2022-23, 2023-24, 2025-26), with little snow. In 2025-26 IMD said WDs travelled at unusually high latitudes and missed the western Himalaya, and that many WDs were moisture-poor with shallow troughs. So in recent years the problem has been weak or misplaced WDs and less snow, more than fewer WDs.
    • Warming also turns snow into rain at lower and middle heights, which shrinks the snowpack even when total precipitation is normal.
[Correction] [Verification Required] No IMD source was found saying that "the frequency of WDs has decreased". The peer-reviewed evidence is mixed, and the largest recent study (Hunt, 2024) found an increase in winter WDs and a longer WD season. Write it as: "WD-linked winter precipitation and snowfall have been erratic and often deficient in recent winters, while WDs are increasingly occurring in late spring and summer."
[Correction] "Arctic warming → slower, meandering jet → weak WDs" is a hypothesis (Arctic amplification), not settled science. The Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the globe since 1979†, which reduces the pole-to-tropics temperature contrast. Some scientists argue this makes the jet slower and wavier. Others find little evidence. For India, Hunt (2024) attributes the WD trend to a stronger subtropical jet. Present it as one proposed mechanism, alongside the observed late retreat of the jet.

3.5 Discussion: Mechanism of WDs and the Effect of Climate Change

The class asked: "Discuss the mechanism of western disturbances and also examine the impact of climate change on western disturbances." A model outline follows.

Introduction. Western disturbances are extra-tropical cyclonic systems (upper-air troughs) that form over the Mediterranean and are carried east by the subtropical westerly jet. They bring most of the winter rain and snow to north-west India and the western Himalaya.

Mechanism. (1) A trough in the wavy westerly jet forms a low over the Mediterranean where cold and warm air meet. (2) In winter the STWJ's southern branch lies south of the Himalaya and carries it east. (3) It picks up moisture from the Mediterranean, Caspian, Black Sea and Arabian Sea. (4) Convergence ahead of the trough and Himalayan uplift give rain on the plains and snow on the hills. (5) Behind it, cold dry north-westerlies bring cold waves and fog. (Map 3, Figure 3.)

Significance. Rabi crops, snowpack and river flows, hydropower, air quality and tourism; but also hail, avalanches and cold waves.

Impact of climate change. (a) Longer WD season: more WDs in May-July because the jet retreats north later, so more clashes with the monsoon and extreme floods (2013, 2023, 2025). (b) Recent dry winters with very little snow (2025-26 among the driest), as weak or high-latitude WDs missed India. (c) Warming shifts snow to rain and speeds up melt, weakening the snowpack. (d) A possible wavier jet from Arctic warming could make WDs stall or divert, but this is debated. (e) Trend studies disagree; one major study finds more winter WDs, not fewer.

Conclusion. WDs are becoming less reliable for the rabi season and the snowpack, and more hazardous out of season. Better WD forecasting linked to crop advisories, glacier and snow monitoring, and climate-resilient wheat varieties are needed.

[Current Affairs] Winter 2025-26: one of the driest on record.
  • North-west India had an 84.8% rainfall deficiency in December 2025. IMD's Director General said WDs did not affect the western Himalaya that winter (Hindustan Times, 11 January 2026).
  • From 1 January to 28 February 2026, all-India rainfall was 59.9% below normal. February 2026 rainfall was the third lowest since 1901, and it was the third warmest February for north-west India (IMD via Hindustan Times, 1 March 2026).
  • Even in a dry season, IMD recorded two successive WDs (29 January to 4 February 2026) that brought rain, snow, hail and dense fog. No major cold wave occurred that week because of the WD activity (IMD press release, 5 February 2026).

4. The Summer (Hot Weather) Season

4.1 Temperature and Pressure

  • March to May (June in the north-west) is the hot-to-hottest season. After the March equinox the sun moves north, so the belt of highest temperature moves north too: about 38°C over the Deccan in March, about 42°C over Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh in April, and 45°C or more over north-west India in May (NCERT)†.
  • Strong heating creates a thermal low over north-west India and Pakistan, which extends east as an elongated trough. The ITCZ moves north. This low later helps draw in the south-west monsoon.
  • Coastal places stay milder, but humid. The Peninsula is cooler than the north because of the sea.
  • Weather of the season (as listed in class): heat waves; the loo; dust storms; thunderstorms; tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea (April-May); and some late western disturbances.

4.2 The Loo

  • What: a hot, dry, dusty, gusty wind that blows in the afternoon over the northern plains, from Punjab to Bihar, strongest between Delhi and Patna, in May and June. It can cause heat stroke.
  • Origin: westerly to north-westerly winds are heated over the Thar desert (in India and Pakistan) and the dry north-west. Intense daytime heating and the steep pressure gradient towards the thermal low make the wind strong in the afternoon.
  • Why no rain: the air is very dry, and sinking air higher up (an upper-level high, linked to the jet) acts as a lid on rising air.
  • The notes say the loo is triggered "more at the Pakistan part of the Thar". [Verification Required] No source was found to confirm this.
[Correction] The notes say "hot and dry condition despite this HP" and "despite hot conditions HP can also be created due to upper-atmospheric sinking". Keep the two levels apart. At the surface, north-west India in May is a thermal low, and the loo blows towards it. In the upper air, a high (anticyclone/ridge) can sit over the region. Its sinking air warms by compression and acts as a lid, so clouds cannot form. That is the heat dome (4.4). The "HP" in the notes is the upper-air high, not surface pressure.

4.3 Local Storms and Pre-monsoon Showers [Additional]

NameRegionNature and importance
LooNorthern plains, Punjab to BiharHot, dry afternoon wind; heat stroke
Andhi / dust stormsRajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, west Uttar PradeshConvective dust storms. They bring a short drop in temperature but damage crops, power lines and visibility.
Nor-westers (Kalbaisakhi, "calamity of Baisakh")West Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, BiharViolent evening thunderstorms with squalls and hail, often arriving from the north-west. They help jute, rice and tea.
Bardoli Chheerha / BordoisilaAssamThe same nor-wester storms in Assam ("tea showers").

Based on NCERT Class 11 India: Physical Environment, Chapter 4†. Kalbaisakhi forms where dry continental air meets moist air from the Bay of Bengal.

4.4 Heat Waves

  • Definition: a heat wave is a period of abnormally high temperature, higher than normal for that place, that is dangerous to human life. IMD judges it by the maximum temperature.
IMD criterionHeat waveSevere heat wave
Pre-conditionMaximum 40°C or more (plains), 37°C or more (coastal stations), 30°C or more (hills)
By departure from normal+4.5°C to +6.4°Cmore than +6.4°C
By actual maximum45°C or more47°C or more
Warm night (needs max 40°C or more)Minimum +4.5°C to +6.4°C above normalVery warm night: more than +6.4°C

Source: IMD - FAQ on Heat Wave. Declared when met at 2 or more stations in a sub-division for 2 consecutive days.

  • Causes (natural): the sun high overhead and long days; clear skies (no clouds); dry, hot north-westerly winds from the Thar; dry soils (little evaporation, so all the energy heats the air); and upper-air highs, heat domes and blocking (below). El Nino years tend to have more heat-wave days.
    [Correction] The notes say "El Nino also causes the heat wave". It is a tendency, not a direct cause. Developing El Nino summers often bring more heat-wave days over India and a weaker monsoon. For example, a 2026 study linked the record May 2026 Indian heat wave to a stronger Iranian Plateau high and Western Pacific Subtropical High during the El Nino developing phase (Gao et al., 2026, Adv. Atmos. Sci.). Heat waves also occur in non-El Nino years.
  • Causes (human): climate change (higher baseline temperatures); deforestation and wetland encroachment (less evaporative cooling); concretisation and urbanisation (the urban heat island, hot nights); and air pollution. Land-use effects are covered in the 14 November note, 6.5.
  • Heat dome: a strong, persistent high pressure in the upper air. Its sinking air warms by compression and acts as a lid, so hot surface air cannot rise to form clouds. With no clouds the ground keeps heating and drying, a feedback that makes the heat wave long-lasting.
  • Omega block: when the westerly jet meanders strongly it can form a loop shaped like the Greek letter omega (Ω). A high sits in the loop with lows on either side, and the pattern stalls for days. Under the high there is a long heat wave, while the flanking lows get heavy rain.
  • Spread: heat waves usually begin over north-west India and spread east and south. The heat-wave-prone area is growing. Maximum frequency is in May, and in June over Bihar, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh†. Kerala, Tamil Nadu, coastal Karnataka and the islands are rarely affected because of maritime air (IMD).

4.5 Short Note: Heat Wave

The class asked for a short note on heat waves.

Meaning: a heat wave is a spell of abnormally high temperature that threatens life. IMD declares one when the maximum reaches at least 40°C (plains), 37°C (coast) or 30°C (hills) and is 4.5°C or more above normal, or when it is 45°C or more.

Causes: intense sun and clear skies in March-June; dry north-westerly winds and the loo; dry soils; upper-air highs, heat domes and omega blocks; El Nino years; and human factors such as global warming, urban heat islands, deforestation and the loss of wetlands.

Impacts: heat stroke and deaths (outdoor workers, the elderly, slum dwellers); warm nights that prevent the body from recovering; lower labour productivity; wheat yield loss from terminal heat; power and water shortages; forest fires.

Response: IMD colour-coded heat-wave warnings; NDMA guidelines and Heat Action Plans (first in Ahmedabad, 2013); heat-wave and lightning relief now allowed from SDRF/NDRF (2026); cool roofs, urban greening and wetland protection; shifted working hours; and early warning through health surveillance.

Conclusion: heat waves are now a recurring disaster. India needs to move from relief to long-term mitigation through heat-resilient cities and health systems.

4.6 Policy: Heat Waves as a Notified Disaster and Heat Action Plans

  • Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan (2013): after the May 2010 heat wave (about 1,344 excess deaths), the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, IIPH Gandhinagar and NRDC launched South Asia's first heat action plan. It has early warnings, inter-agency coordination, hospital preparedness and, later, cool roofs. A 2018 study estimated it avoided about 1,190 deaths a year (Knowlton et al., 2014; ClimaHealth case study). The notes are correct.
  • Heat wave as a notified calamity: the 16th Finance Commission (report submitted 17 November 2025, tabled 1 February 2026) recommended adding heat waves and lightning to the list of notified disasters. The Ministry of Home Affairs then included them in the SDRF/NDRF operational guidelines for 2026-31, and told the Lok Sabha in August 2026. The notified list now has 14 items.
[Correction] The notes say the heat wave was "declared / incorporated into the National Disaster list 2026". More precisely, it was added to the list of notified natural calamities that qualify for SDRF/NDRF funding (operational guidelines for 2026-31). Lightning was added at the same time. Before this, states could notify a heat wave only as a "local disaster" and spend up to 10% of their SDRF on it. India has no separate legal category called a "national disaster".
[Current Affairs] Heat, 2026.
  • Notified calamity: heat waves and lightning were added to the SDRF/NDRF list (MHA reply in Lok Sabha, early August 2026). Between 1 March and 26 July 2026 there were 4,853 heat-stroke cases and 20 confirmed heat-stroke deaths; Telangana reported the most cases (Hindustan Times, 5 August 2026; Down To Earth, 7 August 2026).
  • The 16th Finance Commission noted that 11 states had already declared heat waves a state-specific disaster. It recommended Rs 2,04,401 crore for SDRF and SDMF over 2026-31 (Down To Earth, 2 February 2026).
  • Summer 2026: IMD forecast above-normal heat-wave days for March-May 2026 over east, east-central and south-east India. It also expected a shift from La Nina to neutral and then El Nino. On 18 May 2026 IMD warned of heat-wave to severe heat-wave conditions over north-west and central India; Banda (UP) recorded 46.4°C on 17 May (IMD special bulletin, 18 May 2026).
  • Heat Action Plans: NDMA has asked all states, districts and cities to prepare HAPs. About 300 cities and districts in 23 heat-prone states had them by 2026† (Vajiram, 27 August 2026).

Key Facts for Prelims

  • IMD seasons: Winter Jan-Feb; Pre-monsoon Mar-May; SW monsoon Jun-Sep; Post-monsoon Oct-Dec. The traditional scheme uses Dec-Feb and Oct-Nov.
  • The January 20°C isotherm runs roughly parallel to the Tropic of Cancer. The 18°C January isotherm (Stamp) divides tropical from sub-tropical India.
  • Winter in NW India: surface high, sinking air, calm and stable air, inversions, fog and smog. Land winds are NW in the Ganga valley, N in the delta and NE over the Bay.
  • The NE monsoon gives Tamil Nadu its main rain in Oct-Dec.
  • Formation chain (2.4): sun over the Tropic of Capricorn (22 Dec) → land cools faster than sea → Siberian High + weak NW India high (about 1019 mb vs 1013 mb in the south) → ITCZ shifts to about 5-15°S → NE trades return → STWJ southern branch at about 25°N causes sinking air.
  • Noon sun at Delhi on 22 December: about 38° (about 85° on 21 June).
  • The NE trades become the NW monsoon of northern Australia and Indonesia after crossing the equator.
  • El Nino tends to reduce cold waves in India; La Nina tends to increase them (IMD study, MAUSAM 2022).
  • The STWJ southern branch lies south of the Himalaya at about 9-13 km in winter and steers WDs.
  • WDs: extra-tropical cyclonic systems (upper-air troughs) from the Mediterranean. Moisture comes from the Mediterranean, Black, Caspian and Arabian Seas. There are about 6-7 strong WDs a month in winter.
  • WDs give rain for rabi crops and snow in the western Himalaya; after they pass come cold waves and fog.
  • Cold wave (plains): minimum 10°C or less, and a departure of -4.5 to -6.4°C, or an actual minimum of 4°C or less (severe: 2°C or less).
  • Heat wave: maximum 40°C or more (plains), 37°C or more (coast) or 30°C or more (hills), and a departure of +4.5 to +6.4°C (severe: more than +6.4°C), or an actual maximum of 45°C or more (severe: 47°C or more).
  • Loo: hot, dry afternoon wind, Punjab to Bihar, May-June. Kalbaisakhi: West Bengal (Bardoli Chheerha in Assam). Mango showers: Kerala and coastal Karnataka. Blossom showers: coffee areas.
  • Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan (2013) was South Asia's first.
  • Heat waves and lightning were added to the notified calamities for SDRF/NDRF for 2026-31, on the 16th Finance Commission's recommendation.
  • Hunt (2024): winter WDs over the western and central Himalaya have increased; June WDs are about twice as common in the last 20 years.

Mains Points

  • Mechanism of the winter season: insolation, continentality, the pressure field, the ITCZ shift, the NE trades, the STWJ and the Himalayan barrier, in that order; then regional contrasts and the NE monsoon (model answer in 2.7).
  • Why the winter monsoon is dry: land origin, sinking and stable air, offshore and diverging flow. The Coromandel coast is the exception because the winds cross the Bay of Bengal.
  • WDs and food and water security: rabi wheat, snowpack, summer river flows, hydropower and apple chill hours. Dry winters (2025-26) threaten all of these.
  • Changing behaviour of WDs: a longer season and late-spring and summer WDs, which interact with the monsoon (Kedarnath 2013, north India 2023, Punjab 2025). More rain falls instead of snow. Trend studies disagree.
  • Winter smog in the Indo-Gangetic plain: anticyclonic stability, inversions and low wind speed act as the trap; stubble burning, vehicles and industry are the sources. Rain from WDs clears the air.
  • Heat waves as a disaster: the health and productivity costs, warm nights, humid heat on the coasts, the shift from relief to mitigation (SDRF and SDMF), and the gaps in Heat Action Plans (funding, local capacity).
  • Urban heat: concretisation, loss of wetlands and green cover. Remedies: cool roofs, blue-green infrastructure and better building codes.
  • Heat dome and blocking: they explain why heat waves persist; a possible link to Arctic amplification remains a research question.

Common Traps / Confusions

  • IMD winter = Jan-Feb, not Dec-Feb; IMD post-monsoon = Oct-Dec.
  • WD vs depression: a WD is extra-tropical (a trough in the westerlies); an IMD "depression" is a tropical low stage.
  • Crest = ridge (high aloft); a WD goes with the trough.
  • Surface low vs upper high: in summer NW India has a surface thermal low; the heat dome's high is in the upper air.
  • Cold wave vs cold day: a cold wave is judged on the night minimum; a cold day on the day maximum (fog days).
  • NE monsoon vs WD: Tamil Nadu's winter rain is the NE monsoon; Punjab's winter rain is from WDs.
  • NE monsoon vs NE trades: they are the same wind system. It is dry over most of India and wet only where it has crossed the Bay of Bengal.
  • Siberian High vs NW India high: the Siberian High is very strong but is mostly blocked by the Himalaya; the NW India high is weak (about 1019 mb).
  • El Nino and winter: El Nino weakens the SW monsoon but tends to give fewer cold waves in winter; La Nina tends to give harsher cold waves.
  • The westerlies blow between 30° and 60° in each hemisphere, not "30°N-60°S" (PYQ 1).
  • Kalbaisakhi is in West Bengal, not Tamil Nadu. Mango showers are in Kerala and Karnataka, not Bengal.
  • Heat waves were added to the SDRF/NDRF notified calamities; there is no legal "national disaster" label.
  • "WD frequency is falling" is not established; winter precipitation has often been deficient.

30-Second Revision

Winter: sun south → land cools, Siberian High + NW high → ITCZ to 5-15S, NE trades → cold NW high, sinking air, calm → dry land winds, fog/smog + STWJ south branch → WDs from the Mediterranean → rain/snow, then cold wave
Summer: sun north → heat belt Deccan→MP→NW → thermal low, loo, andhi, nor-westers → heat dome/omega block = long heat waves → HAPs + SDRF (2026)

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Wording follows the official papers as given in reputable compilations; questions marked "near-exact" were taken from compilations and could not be matched to the official paper word for word.

1. UPSC CSE Prelims 2015 - General Studies Paper I

Consider the following statements:
1. The winds which blow between 30° N and 60° S latitudes throughout the year are known as westerlies.
2. The moist air masses that cause winter rains in North-Western region of India are part of westerlies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

  1. 1 only
  2. 2 only
  3. Both 1 and 2
  4. Neither 1 nor 2

Answer: (b) 2 only. The westerlies blow between 30° and 60° in each hemisphere. The winter rain of NW India comes from western disturbances carried by the westerlies (3.2).

2. UPSC CSE Prelims 2020 - General Studies Paper I

Consider the following statements:
1. Jet streams occur in the Northern Hemisphere only.
2. Only some cyclones develop an eye.
3. The temperature inside the eye of a cyclone is nearly 10°C lesser than that of the surroundings.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

  1. 1 only
  2. 2 and 3 only
  3. 2 only
  4. 1 and 3 only

Answer: (c) 2 only. Jet streams occur in both hemispheres, and the eye of a cyclone is warmer than its surroundings, not cooler. The STWJ that steers WDs is one of these jets (2.2).

3. UPSC CSE Prelims 2024 - General Studies Paper I (near-exact)

Which of the following is/are correct inference/inferences from isothermal maps in the month of January?
1. The isotherms deviate to the north over the ocean and to the south over the continent.
2. The presence of cold ocean currents, Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift make the North Atlantic Ocean colder and the isotherms bend towards the north.
Select the answer using the code given below:

  1. 1 only
  2. 2 only
  3. Both 1 and 2
  4. Neither 1 nor 2

Answer: (a) 1 only. In the northern winter the continents are colder than the oceans, so isotherms bend south over land. The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift are warm currents. This is the same continentality that makes north India cold in winter (2.1).

4. UPSC CSE Prelims 1997 - General Studies (near-exact)

The January isotherm taken as a basis for dividing India into tropical and sub-tropical zones is:

  1. 21°C
  2. 18°C
  3. 12°C
  4. 15°C

Answer: (b) 18°C. Stamp's 18°C January isotherm separates tropical from sub-tropical India. Do not mix it up with the 20°C isotherm in the notes (2.1).

5. UPSC CSE Mains 2013 - General Studies Paper I (10 marks, two parts)

(a) Bring out the causes for the formation of heat islands in the urban habitat of the world. (b) What do you understand by the phenomenon of 'temperature inversion' in meteorology? How does it affect weather and the habitants of the place?

Approach: (a) low-albedo concrete and asphalt, less vegetation and evaporation, waste heat, urban canyons and the pollution dome; these make urban heat waves worse (4.4). (b) Inversion is the reversal of the normal lapse rate. It forms on calm, clear winter nights and under subsiding air. It stops convection and traps fog and smog, as in north Indian winters (2.2, Figure 1).

6. UPSC CSE Mains 2026 - General Studies Paper I (near-exact; English rendering of a Hindi-medium listing)

Compare the Loo, Chinook and Foehn winds with reference to their regions of prevalence, their nature and their climatic effects.

Approach: the Loo is a hot, dry wind of the north Indian plains in May-June, heated over a dry interior (4.2). The Chinook (Rockies) and Foehn (Alps) are warm, dry winds that descend leeward slopes and warm by compression. They melt snow ("snow eater") and are useful for grazing. The Loo causes heat stroke. Corrections Made

Each link returns to the explanation, which keeps the original rough-note claim.

  1. IMD seasons are Jan-Feb, Mar-May, Jun-Sep, Oct-Dec; Dec-Feb / Oct-Nov is the traditional scheme.
  2. Cold waves mostly follow the passage of a WD (cold NW winds, clear skies, snow on the hills), not just Central Asian air.
  3. A WD is an extra-tropical upper-air trough, not a "depression" in IMD's tropical sense.
  4. Crest and ridge are the same; a WD is tied to the trough.
  5. No IMD source says WD frequency has fallen; evidence is mixed, and one major study finds an increase. Winter precipitation has been deficient.
  6. "Arctic warming → slower, wavier jet → weak WDs" is a debated hypothesis.
  7. The surface in NW India in summer is a thermal low; the heat-dome high is in the upper air.
  8. El Nino favours more heat waves but does not by itself cause them.
  9. Heat waves (and lightning) were added to the SDRF/NDRF notified calamities for 2026-31, not to a "national disaster" list.
